status: drafted via multi-agent workflow grounded in the real extracted verse text, adversarially fact-checked and corrected
notes: 1 Maccabees is unique to the Geneva translation (deuterocanonical/apocryphal; not in the KJV Character Index) and is continuous political-military narrative history covering roughly 175-134 BC, so unlike Leviticus/Deuteronomy this book needed zero law/theme tiers — every tier is person-type, including the institution of the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah) at 4:36-59, which stays embedded in Judas Maccabaeus's own tier rather than becoming a separate law tier, since he personally leads the cleansing and personally institutes the feast (the "personally embodied" test, not "pure transmission"). Structure follows the book's own five-generation Hasmonean succession (Mattathias -> Judas -> Jonathan -> Simon -> John) plus the churning cast of Seleucid kings and generals who oppose or ally with them. Real naming collisions found and deliberately kept separate, never merged: two men named Judas (Judas Maccabaeus vs. Simon's son Judas, killed with him at 16:16); two named Mattathias (the patriarch vs. Simon's son, also killed at 16:16); two named Apollonius (the governor Judas kills at 3:10-12 vs. the later governor of Coelesyria under Demetrius II at 10:69-84); at least three distinct men called Ptolemy (the unnamed king of Egypt in ch.1, Ptolemy son of Dorymenes the Syrian general at 3:38, and Ptolemy son of Abubus who murders Simon at 16:11-16) plus a possible fourth if the Ptolemy of ch.1 and the Ptolemy of ch.10-11 are not the same man - the text itself never confirms or denies this, so it is left unresolved rather than assumed; two kings named Demetrius, distinguished by the text only via patronymic ("son of Seleucus" at 7:1 vs. "son of Demetrius" at 10:67), so neither is called "I"/"II" or "Soter"/"Nicator" in this book - those numbering conventions are external and are avoided as character names here, used only in scribeTier flavor text where unambiguous. Four distinct figures named Antiochus appear: Antiochus Epiphanes and Antiochus Eupator both carry real textual epithets (1:10, 6:17) so those names are used directly; the young son of Alexander (11:39-40) and the "Antiochus, son of Demetrius" who writes from the isles in ch.15 have no textual epithet, so they are named descriptively rather than assigned the external "VI"/"VII Sidetes" numbering. Ch.15:1's phrase "son of Demetrius the king" is itself ambiguous about which Demetrius is meant - flagged rather than resolved. "John" (Simon's surviving son, ch.13-16) is never called "Hyrcanus" anywhere in this text; that surname is a later historical title and is deliberately not used as part of his indexed name. Background/non-recurring figures (Alexander the Great's death and division of his empire at 1:1-9; the unnamed "king of Egypt" defeated by Antiochus Epiphanes at 1:16-19; the earlier high priest Onias's exchange of letters with the Spartan king Arius, quoted at 12:7-8) are logged in genealogyLists rather than given full character entries, since they do not recur as active participants in the ongoing Hasmonean-Seleucid conflict this book actually tracks.

characters.name: Mattathias

genealogy.father: John, son of Simeon, a priest of the sons of Joarib — named only via patronymic in the text, 1 Maccabees 2:1

verses.note: Introduced as a priest of the line of Joarib, dwelling at Modin.
Kills the Jew who steps forward to sacrifice on the king's altar, and the king's officer enforcing it, then pulls down the altar — the revolt's opening act of zeal.
Cries 'Whosoever is zealous for the law...let him come forth after me,' and flees into the mountains with his sons.
On his deathbed, exhorts his sons to zeal for the law, names Simon as counselor and Judas as military leader, then dies and is buried at Modin in the 146th year.

funFacts: His five sons each carried a surname besides their own — John Gaddis, Simon Thassi, Judas Maccabaeus, Eleazar Avaran, and Jonathan Apphus (1 Maccabees 2:2-5).

characters.name: Judas Maccabaeus

verses.note: Rises up in his father's stead, likened to 'a lion's whelp roaring for prey.'
Defeats and kills Apollonius (the governor), taking his sword and fighting with it ever after.
Leads the cleansing and rededication of the defiled sanctuary, builds a new altar, and institutes the eight-day Feast of Dedication to be kept 'from year to year' — the origin of Hanukkah.
Defeats and kills Nicanor at Adasa; his head and hand are hung up beside Jerusalem, commemorated as an annual feast day.
Refuses to flee an overwhelming force at Elasa ('let us die manfully for our brethren's sake'), and is killed in the battle; buried by his brothers at Modin.

funFacts: The Feast of Dedication he instituted (1 Maccabees 4:59) is the origin of Hanukkah.

verses.note: Named among Mattathias's five sons, surnamed Avaran.

Believing a royal-armored elephant carries the king, charges alone into the phalanx, stabs it from beneath, and is crushed to death when it falls on him — 'he gave himself to deliver his people, and to get him an everlasting name.'

children: two unnamed sons handed over as hostages to Tryphon, 1 Maccabees 13:16 — the text never names them or records their fate afterward

verses.note: Named among Mattathias's five sons, surnamed Apphus.
Chosen by the people to succeed Judas as leader after his death.
Appointed high priest by King Alexander and formally puts on the holy garments at the Feast of Tabernacles.
Lured to Ptolemais by Tryphon under a pretense of friendship, then seized; those who entered with him are put to the sword.
Killed by Tryphon near Bascama despite Simon's ransom payment; buried by Simon at Modin.
Named among Mattathias's five sons, surnamed Thassi.
Acclaimed leader by the people after Jonathan's capture: 'Thou art our leader instead of Judas and Jonathan thy brother.'
Judaea is freed from Seleucid tribute in the 170th year; documents begin to be dated 'in the first year of Simon.'
Sends a thousand-pound gold shield to Rome to renew the alliance; Rome circulates letters on Judaea's behalf to many nations.
Murdered along with two of his sons at a banquet in the stronghold of Dok by his own son-in-law, Ptolemy son of Abubus.

characters.name: John, son of Simon

verses.note: Simon makes him leader of all his forces; he dwells at Gazara.
Warns his father of Cendebaeus's advance; Simon commissions him and his brother Judas to take up the family's wars.
Leads the rout of Cendebaeus's army, pursuing them to Kidron and Azotus.
Warned in time at Gazara that his father and brothers have been murdered and that he is next; kills the men sent to assassinate him.
The book closes noting his further acts are 'written in the chronicles of his high priesthood.'

funFacts: The text never calls him 'Hyrcanus' — only 'John.' That surname is a later historical title, not found in this book, so it is not asserted here as part of his textual name.

genealogy.father: Antiochus the king (the text's own phrase, 1:10; whether the 'hostage at Rome' clause describes the father or Epiphanes himself is left ambiguous by the Geneva wording)

verses.note: Called 'a sinful root'; begins to reign in the 137th year of the Greek kingdom.
After conquering Egypt, enters the sanctuary at Jerusalem and strips the golden altar, candlestick, table, and vessels.
Decrees that all his kingdom become 'one people,' forbidding Jewish worship, sabbaths, and circumcision on pain of death.
Sets up 'the abomination of desolation' upon the altar on the 15th of Chislev, 145th year.
Falls sick with grief on hearing his forces in Judah were routed and the temple purified; dies in a strange land, confessing 'these evils are come upon me.'

Described as 'an honourable man, and one of the seed royal'; left to govern from the Euphrates to Egypt's border, given half the royal forces, and charged to raise Antiochus's son and destroy Judah's strength.
Leads sixty thousand chosen footmen against Judas at Bethsura; his army is routed with 5,000 dead.
Musters a still larger force with war elephants and besieges the sanctuary alongside King Antiochus Eupator, but withdraws to make peace on hearing Philip has seized Antioch.
Brought before the new king Demetrius, who orders 'Shew me not their faces' — Lysias and young Antiochus are put to death by the army.
Sent by Demetrius, 'a man that hated Israel and was their enemy,' commanded to destroy the people.
Mocks the priests offering sacrifice for the king and swears in rage to burn the temple unless Judas is delivered to him.
Killed first in the battle at Adasa; his head and outstretched right hand are cut off and hung up beside Jerusalem.
His defeat is commemorated yearly on the 13th of Adar.
'One of the king's Friends, ruler in the country beyond the river'; sent with Alcimus to install him as high priest and take vengeance on Israel.
Slays sixty Hasidaeans who trusted his oath of peace; later casts many deserters into 'the great pit' at Bezeth.
Returns with Alcimus and defeats Judas's much-diminished force at Elasa; Judas is killed.
Besieges Jonathan and Simon at Bethbasi but is discomfited by Simon's sortie; makes peace with Jonathan and departs, and 'the sword ceased from Israel.'

characters.name: Demetrius, son of Seleucus

verses.note: Comes from Rome, seizes the throne, and orders Antiochus Eupator and Lysias killed unseen: 'Shew me not their faces.'
Sends Nicanor against Judas after Alcimus's accusations.
Sends Bacchides and Alcimus back into Judah a second time after Nicanor's death.
Gathers forces against the rival claimant Alexander; is defeated and falls in battle.

funFacts: Later tradition calls him 'Demetrius I Soter,' a title this book never uses — it distinguishes him from the second Demetrius only by patronymic ('son of Seleucus').

characters.name: Alexander Epiphanes

genealogy.father: Antiochus (per the text's own claim, 1 Maccabees 10:1, 'Alexander Epiphanes, the son of Antiochus' — presented without further comment)
spouses: Cleopatra, daughter of Ptolemy (King of Egypt) — married at Ptolemais 'with great pomp,' 1 Maccabees 10:57-58, later taken back by her father and given to Demetrius instead, 11:12

verses.note: Takes Ptolemais and reigns there, styled 'Alexander Epiphanes, the son of Antiochus.'
Writes to Jonathan calling him 'brother' and 'Friend,' appoints him high priest, and sends a purple robe and gold crown.
Defeats and kills Demetrius in battle, taking the kingdom.
Defeated in turn by Ptolemy's forces, flees into Arabia, and is beheaded by Zabdiel the Arabian.

funFacts: Later tradition calls him 'Alexander Balas,' a name this book never uses — it consistently calls him 'Alexander' or 'Alexander Epiphanes.'

characters.name: Demetrius, son of Demetrius

verses.note: Comes out of Crete into the land of his fathers, styled 'Demetrius, son of Demetrius.'
Begins to reign in the 167th year after Ptolemy's death.
Disbands most of his forces except foreign troops, is nearly killed in an Antiochene uprising, and is saved only when Jonathan sends 3,000 Jewish soldiers to fight for him.
Marches into Media to raise help against Tryphon; is captured alive by Arsaces' general and held prisoner.

funFacts: Later tradition calls him 'Demetrius II Nicator' — this book distinguishes him from his father only by the shared bare name plus patronymic.

verses.note: Formerly of Alexander's party; seeks out the young child Antiochus from Imalcue the Arabian, intending to make him king in his father's place.
Lures Jonathan to Ptolemais with a false promise of handing over the city, then seizes him and slaughters his escort.
Has Jonathan killed near Bascama after Simon's ransom fails to secure his release.
Deals treacherously with the young King Antiochus, kills him, and reigns in his place, putting on the diadem of Asia.
Flees by ship to Orthosia after Antiochus (son of Demetrius) drives him out of Dor.

characters.name: Antiochus, son of Demetrius

genealogy.father: Demetrius the king (1 Maccabees 15:1 — the phrase 'son of Demetrius the king' does not itself specify whether this is Demetrius I or Demetrius II, i.e. whether he is Demetrius II's brother or son, by the book's own wording)

verses.note: Sends letters from the isles of the sea confirming Simon's privileges and coinage rights, seeking Jewish support to reclaim the kingdom from Tryphon.
Lands, gathers the kingdom's forces, and besieges Tryphon in Dor by land and sea.
Rejects Simon's sent aid, and through Athenobius demands the return of Joppa, Gazara, and the citadel, or 500 talents plus 500 more for damages.
Appoints Cendebaeus captain of the sea coast to harass Judaea while he himself pursues Tryphon.

funFacts: Later tradition calls him 'Antiochus VII Sidetes' — neither the number nor the epithet 'Sidetes' appears in this book.

spouses: an unnamed daughter of Simon — implied by 'he was the high priest's son in law,' 1 Maccabees 16:12

verses.note: Appointed captain of the plain of Jericho, wealthy, and Simon's own son-in-law; secretly plots to seize control of the country.
Hosts Simon and two of his sons at a banquet in the stronghold of Dok, and murders them once they are drunk.
Writes to the king for reinforcements and sends men to kill John at Gazara too, but John is warned in time.
Set up as king by Lysias after his father's death; given the name Eupator.
Personally besieges the sanctuary with Lysias, then withdraws after making and immediately breaking an oath of peace, ordering the wall of Sion pulled down.
Executed on Demetrius's order alongside Lysias, unseen.

characters.name: Ptolemy (King of Egypt)

children: Cleopatra, given in marriage to Alexander, later given instead to Demetrius, 1 Maccabees 10:57-58, 11:12

verses.note: Answers Alexander's request for a marriage alliance favorably; gives his daughter Cleopatra to him at Ptolemais.
Marches into Syria under pretense of friendship, garrisons cities, then takes Cleopatra back from Alexander and gives her to Demetrius instead, taking both the Egyptian and Asian diadems for himself.
Receives Alexander's severed head from Zabdiel the Arabian; dies himself three days later.

funFacts: Traditionally identified as Ptolemy VI Philometor from external history, but the text never numbers him — it only ever calls him 'Ptolemy' or 'the king of Egypt.'

verses.note: Beheads the fleeing Alexander and sends his head to Ptolemy.

characters.name: Apollonius (governor of Coelesyria)

verses.note: Appointed by Demetrius over Coelesyria; taunts Jonathan to come down and fight him in the plain.
Defeated at Azotus; his hidden ambush of a thousand horse fails, and Jonathan burns the temple of Dagon at Azotus where his fleeing men took refuge.

funFacts: A different man from the earlier Apollonius whom Judas kills in chapter 3 — the book never links the two.

characters.name: Antiochus (the young king)

verses.note: Nourished by Imalcue the Arabian; Tryphon seeks him out to install as king.
Reigns as young Antiochus; confirms Jonathan's high priesthood and honors, appoints Simon captain from the Ladder of Tyre to Egypt's border.
Murdered by Tryphon, who then takes the throne for himself.

funFacts: Traditionally numbered 'Antiochus VI' by later historians — this book calls him only 'Antiochus' or 'the young child Antiochus.'

verses.note: Sent to demand Joppa, Gazara, and the citadel back from Simon; is shown Simon's wealth and glory, and reports back to the enraged king empty-handed.
Appointed captain of the sea coast; builds up Kidron and raids Judaea's roads.
Defeated by John and Judas, Simon's sons, at the brook near Modin; flees to the stronghold, losing about 2,000 men.

characters.name: Apollonius (the governor)

verses.note: Gathers Gentile forces and a great host from Samaria against Israel; defeated and killed by Judas, who takes his sword as his own weapon.

funFacts: A different man from the later Apollonius, governor of Coelesyria under Demetrius (chapter 10) — the book never links the two.

verses.note: Commander of the Syrian host who seeks glory by crushing Judas's small company at Bethhoron; routed instead, losing about 800 men.
Leads a night raid meant to surprise Judas's camp at Emmaus, but finds it empty; his own camp is burned by Judas while he searches the mountains.
Leads a mighty Ammonite band against Judas; discomfited and pursued to Jazer.
Gathers another army at Raphon with hired Arabians; routed a second time, fleeing to the temple at Carnaim, which Judas burns.
Left with Azarias as leader of the remnant force in Judaea, under strict orders not to fight while Judas and Simon are away.
Disobeys, seeking his own glory, and is routed by Gorgias's men at Jamnia with about 2,000 dead — 'they were not of the seed of those men, by whose hand deliverance was given unto Israel.'
Co-leader with Joseph son of Zacharias of the home-front force; shares in the disastrous defeat at Jamnia.

characters.name: Judas, son of Simon

verses.note: Called by his father, alongside his brother John, to take up the family's wars: 'be ye instead of me and my brother.'
Accompanies Simon to Jericho and is murdered alongside him at Ptolemy's banquet.

funFacts: A different man from Judas Maccabaeus — the book never links the two beyond the shared name.

characters.name: Mattathias, son of Simon

verses.note: Travels with Simon and his brother Judas to Jericho in the 177th year.
Murdered alongside his father at the banquet in Dok.

funFacts: A different man from the patriarch Mattathias — the book never links the two beyond the shared name.

verses.note: Named as Mattathias's eldest son, surnamed Gaddis.
Sent to the Nabathaeans with the brothers' baggage; captured and carried off by the children of Jambri from Medaba.
Avenged by Jonathan and Simon, who ambush the wedding party of Jambri's sons and destroy them; John himself does not reappear afterward.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk/background references, kept out of the character list above since they do not recur as active participants in the ongoing Hasmonean-Seleucid conflict this book tracks.

alexanderTheGreat.note: Scene-setting background only: Alexander the Macedonian defeats Darius, conquers widely, divides his kingdom among his servants on his deathbed, and dies after a 12-year reign — the origin point of the successor Greek kingdoms the rest of the book plays out under.

ptolemyKingOfEgyptCh1.note: An unnamed 'Ptolemy king of Egypt,' defeated and put to flight by Antiochus Epiphanes' invasion of Egypt. The text never confirms whether this is the same individual as the later 'Ptolemy, king of Egypt' who appears as Alexander's father-in-law in chapters 10-11 (indexed there as ptolemy_vi_philometor_geneva1macc) — left unresolved rather than assumed, since decades and several chapters separate the two mentions.

oniasAndArius.note: An earlier high priest, Onias, is said to have received a letter from Arius, king of the Spartans, claiming Jewish-Spartan kinship 'of the stock of Abraham' — quoted by Jonathan in his own letter to the Spartans as historical precedent for renewing friendship. Neither Onias nor Arius is an active participant in this book's main narrative, so both are logged here rather than as full characters.
